phonemes.desc: Short upsilon [y] — a rounded, front vowel like French "u" — the whirlwind's first breath.
Aspirated phi [pʰ] followed by long omega [ɔː] and nu; the name roars and sustains.

pronunciation.approximation: "tee-FOHN" — but the first vowel is like French "tu," and the second is long and breathy, like a storm that does not end quickly.

pronunciation.note: Typhōn is Tier 1 because the Greek Τυφῶν contains both stress and length: the circumflex over the omega marks a long vowel that also carries the pitch peak. The single character ῶ encodes both features, and the macron form Typhōn preserves the long vowel while implying the original stress position. The name sounds like what it describes: a long, smoky exhalation.

domains.title: The Father of Monsters
domains.subtitle: Storms, Fire, Rebellion
domains.lead: Typhōn is the last thing the Olympians feared. Born from Gaia and the abyss, he is a serpentine giant with a hundred heads, voices of gods and beasts, and fire blazing from his eyes. He is the cosmic rebel who nearly unmade Zeus's order.

cards.name: The Hundred Heads
cards.desc: Each head speaks a different tongue — bull, lion, god, snake — a cacophony of chaos.

cards.name: Fire and Etna
cards.desc: Buried beneath Mount Etna, his breath becomes volcanic eruption; Sicily trembles at his struggles.

cards.name: The Typhon Winds
cards.desc: From him spring the destructive storm winds — the whirlwinds that wreck ships and harvests.

cards.name: Progeny of Monsters
cards.desc: With Echidna he fathers Cerberus, Hydra, Chimera, Sphinx, Nemean Lion — the adversaries of heroes.

symbols.name: Hundred serpent heads
symbols.meaning: Chaos of voices and the many faces of destruction

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The speed of storm and the reach of rebellion

symbols.name: Mount Etna
symbols.meaning: His prison and his continuing presence in the world

mythology.lead: Typhōn is the final adversary in the Greek succession myth, the storm born when the earth has no gods left to raise against heaven. After the Titans fall, Gaia produces one last monster to challenge the new king of the gods — and this time, Hesiod admits, the gods themselves run.

myths.title: Son of Earth and Abyss
myths.text: Hesiod writes that after Zeus drove the Titans from heaven, Gaia lay with Tártaros — 'through golden Aphrodité', the Theogony says — and bore her last and most terrible child: Typhōn, 'the mind-baffling' monster 'who would have ruled over mortals and immortals' had Zeus not acted first (Hesiod, Theogony 820–835). Apollodorus adds the motive: Gaia conceived him in anger at the destruction of her other brood, the Giants, so that the final challenger of the new order is literally the earth's revenge (Apollodorus, Library 1.6.3). Everything about the birth reverses the usual pattern of the succession myth. Where Kronos and Zeus were gods who became kings, Typhōn is a force that would unmake kingship; where the earlier wars pitted generation against generation, this one pits order against the chthonic storm itself. The Theogony's meaning is plain: Zeus's cosmos was won, not given — and the earth keeps one more child in reserve against every heaven.

myths.title: The Typhonomachy
myths.text: The battle shook the cosmos. Hesiod piles up the horror: a hundred serpent heads grew from Typhōn's shoulders, each speaking with a different voice — the speech of gods, the bellowing of bulls, the roars of lions, the baying of hounds, the hissing of serpents — while fire blazed from his eyes and 'a flaming monster' boiled the sea and scorched the earth beneath the thunder of Zeus's reply (Theogony 820–868). The whole arsenal of Olympus — thunderbolts forged by the Cyclopes, winds sealed in Tartarus — went into the storm, until the monster, his hundred heads broken and his strength consumed, was hurled down crippled into the pit. Later poets measured the terror by the gods' flight: in Ovid's version the Olympians fled to Egypt and hid in animal shapes, Zeus himself a ram, until the danger passed (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.319–331). The myth means that heaven survived this time — but only just, and the smoke never fully cleared.

myths.title: Zeus Disarmed
myths.text: Apollodorus preserves the more perilous version of the war, in which Olympus nearly lost. In the first engagement Typhōn won: he cut the sinews from Zeus's hands and feet, hid them in a bearskin, and stowed them in a Cilician cave guarded by the she-serpent Delphine, leaving the king of the gods a helpless trunk (Apollodorus 1.6.3). Rescue came from the margins of the pantheon — Hermes and Aegipan stole the sinews back and refitted them to Zeus, and the war resumed. Now it was pursuit across the whole map: Typhōn fled to Mount Nysa, where the Moirai tricked him with ephemeral fruits; to Thrace, spattering the Haemus range with blood; and at last to Sicily, where Zeus crushed him under Mount Etna or hurled him back into Tartarus — the sources differ, and both prisons stuck. The myth's quiet lesson is the one mythology rarely admits: sovereignty depends on coalition, and the king of the gods rules only because the trickster and the goat-god once went into the cave for him.

myths.title: Father of Monsters
myths.text: With Echidna — 'the mother of gods' adversaries', half nymph and half snake — Typhōn produced the great monsters of Greek myth. Hesiod names Orthrus, the two-headed hound; Cerberus, the hound of Hades; the Lernaean Hydra; and the fire-breathing Chimera, lion before, serpent behind, goat between (Theogony 306–319). Apollodorus extends the family to the Sphinx, the Nemean Lion, the Crommyonian Sow, the eagle that tormented Prometheus, and the sleepless dragon that guarded the Golden Fleece (Library 2–3, passim); the Homeric Hymn to Apollo makes the she-dragon of Delphi their daughter as well (Hymn to Apollo 300 ff.). The catalogue is the point: nearly every labor imposed on Heracles, every ordeal of Jason or Oedipus, belongs to this one marriage. The war of order against chaos is not an episode but an inheritance — Typhōn's children keep the rebellion going generation after generation, so that every hero's victory is, in the long genealogy, one more battle in the Typhonomachy.

myths.title: The Music Against the Monster
myths.text: The last great telling of the war is also the strangest, and it comes half a millennium after Hesiod. In Nonnus's Dionysiaca (1.481–2.620, fifth century CE), Typhōn rises again and once more steals the sinews of Zeus, hiding them in the Corycian cave; the god of gods lies helpless, and the monster bargains for the scepter of heaven and the bride Harmonia. The rescue falls to a mortal wanderer: Cadmus of Thebes, still searching the seas for his abducted sister Europa, takes up his pipes and plays a music so beguiling that the hundred heads of Typhōn nod and sleep one by one, while the sinews are lifted from under him. Zeus wakes, hurls his bolts, and pins the monster under a Sicilian crag. Nonnus knew he was amplifying — his epic calls back to Hesiod by name — and he makes the old myth new by changing its hero: where Apollodorus needed Hermes and a goat-god, late antiquity sends a musician. The late myth says what the early ones imply: chaos is never killed, only ever lulled, and the instrument that lulls it is art.

lore.syncretism: From the fifth century BCE onward, Greeks identified Typhōn with the Egyptian god Set, the red-haired storm deity who murdered Osiris — an equation already active in Herodotus (Histories 2) that may have shaped Typhōn's later iconography of wings, desert wind, and serpent legs. Near Eastern storm-gods — Hittite Taru, Canaanite Baal in his conflict with the sea — may lie behind the Greek figure's oldest layer, though the borrowing is debated. The Romans kept the name Typhon and used it for whirlwinds and eruptions, especially in Sicily. In Egypt the equation hardened into theology: Set-Typhon became the archetype of the impious rebel, and the name 'Typhon' passed into Greek magical papyri and gnostic texts as a title for the forces of chaos.
lore.culturalLegacy: Typhōn gave his name to the typhoon, one of the most feared words in meteorology — though the route may run through Arabic ṭūfān and Chinese taifeng as well as Greek, and scholars still argue the etymology. In fantasy, 'Typhon' names ancient dragons, sea monsters, and final bosses; Dungeons & Dragons, video games, and anime have made him a staple of world-ending antagonists. Geologically, Mount Etna's eruptions were long explained as Typhōn's breath or struggles, and the volcano keeps his name in the guidebooks of Sicily. The monster remains the archetype of the rebellion that almost succeeded — the figure every subsequent cosmic villain, from Milton's Satan to the kaiju of modern film, is descended from.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Typhōn is what the ordered world keeps under the mountain. He is the hundred-headed argument against hierarchy, the storm that rises when the earth decides the gods have gone too far. Every pantheon needs such a figure: not a villain with a motive, but a force so large it can threaten heaven itself.

The Greeks did not kill Typhōn; they buried him alive. That is the most honest thing they could have done. To destroy him would be to pretend chaos can be eliminated; to imprison him is to admit it must be continuously held down. The smoke of Etna is the reminder: the monster is still breathing.
lore.archaeology: Typhon is best attested in mythic art rather than cult. The sixth-century BCE Chalcidian hydria in the Louvre shows Zeus battling Typhon. The Pergamon Altar's Gigantomachy includes snaky-legged opponents evoking the monster. Sicily's volcanic Mount Etna and the caves near Catania were identified as Typhon's prison. Apulian and South Italian vases depict the defeated Typhon beneath Etna or in the underworld.
